cards.text: A poet is grieving over Jerusalem, and he calls the city the Daughter of Zion. And from the very first line, he wants you to know who is behind all this.

cards.question: The poet says the Lord has covered the Daughter of Zion with the cloud of His ___.

cards.text: He has cast the glory of Israel from heaven to earth, and abandoned His footstool in the day of His anger. Friend, I once dropped a whole tray of cookies off the top rack in my bakery and called it a disaster. I need a new word.

cards.question: Next the Lord swallows up all the dwellings of Jacob. How does the poet say He does it?

cards.text: In His wrath He tears down the fortified cities of the Daughter of Judah, and brings her kingdom and its princes to the ground. Friend, this poet does NOT ease you in.

cards.question: In fierce anger the Lord has cut off every horn of Israel. Then, as the enemy approaches, the poet says the Lord has ___ His right hand.

cards.text: Then He burns in Jacob like a flaming fire that eats up everything around it. I've spent my whole life next to ovens, friend, and I've never seen heat like that.

cards.question: Now the poet pictures the Lord with a weapon. Like an enemy, He has bent His ___.
After swallowing up Israel's palaces and strongholds, the Lord has multiplied feasting and songs for the Daughter of Judah.

cards.text: Then it hits the holiest place of all. He lays waste His own tabernacle like a garden booth and destroys His place of meeting.

cards.question: With His place of meeting destroyed, what has the LORD made Zion forget?
In His fierce anger, the Lord has despised the king but spared the priest.

cards.text: The Lord rejects His altar, abandons His sanctuary and hands the walls of her palaces over to the enemy. Friend, that's His OWN altar.

cards.question: Now the enemy raises a shout in the house of the LORD. What does the poet say it sounds like?

answers.text: The day of an appointed feast

cards.text: The LORD determined to destroy the wall of the Daughter of Zion and stretched out a measuring line, and He made even the ramparts and walls lament. When the WALLS are crying, friend, it's serious.

cards.question: With her gates sunk into the ground and her king exiled among the nations, the poet says the law is no more.
Even Zion's prophets are hit. What do they find from the LORD?

cards.text: The elders of the Daughter of Zion sit on the ground in silence, with dust on their heads and sackcloth on. I know that kind of quiet, friend, from my years in the back of that junk drawer.
Now the poet speaks for himself: "My eyes fail from weeping; I am churning within." His heart is poured out in grief over the destruction of his people.

cards.question: The poet's heart is poured out in grief because children and infants ___ in the streets of the city.

cards.text: They faint like the wounded in the streets, and their lives fade away in their mothers' arms. Friend, I'm not going to dress this one up.

cards.question: As they faint in the streets, what do the children cry out to their mothers?

answers.text: Where is the grain and wine
When will our fathers come home
Where did all the soldiers go

cards.text: The poet turns to the Daughter of Jerusalem and searches for something to compare her to, so he can console her. I don't run out of words much, friend, but this would do it.

cards.question: The poet tells the Daughter of Zion that her wound is small and will heal soon.

cards.text: He says her wound is as deep as the sea, and asks who could ever heal her. Then he turns to her prophets.

cards.question: What does the poet say about the visions of Zion's prophets?

answers.text: They were too hard to understand

cards.question: Zion's prophets exposed her guilt to ward off her captivity.

cards.text: Now everyone who passes by claps their hands at the Daughter of Jerusalem in scorn, hissing and shaking their heads. Friend, that's not a crowd. That's a heckling section.

cards.question: Shaking their heads at the Daughter of Jerusalem, what do the passersby ask?

answers.text: Is this the city called the perfection of beauty
Is this the city that once ruled the nations
Is this the city with the tallest walls

cards.text: All her enemies open their mouths against her too. They hiss, gnash their teeth and say, "We have swallowed her up." Friend, there's that word swallowed again.

cards.question: What else do Zion's enemies say about this day?

answers.text: It is the day they have waited for
It took them all by surprise
It is a day they will regret

cards.text: Then the poet says the LORD has done what He planned, overthrowing her without pity and exalting the horn of her foes. Read that one slow, friend.

cards.question: The poet says the decree the LORD accomplished was one He had only just decided on.

cards.text: The hearts of the people cry out to the Lord, and the poet tells the wall of the Daughter of Zion to let its tears run down like a river. Told you those walls were crying, friend.

cards.question: How long does the poet tell the wall of the Daughter of Zion to let its tears run?
The poet says to cry out in the night and pour out your heart like water. In whose presence?
The poet says to lift up your hands to the Lord for the lives of your ___ who are fainting from hunger on every street corner.

cards.text: Then the poet speaks straight to God: "Look, O LORD, and consider: Whom have You ever treated like this?" He even asks whether women should eat the infants they have nurtured.

cards.question: In his prayer, the poet asks whether priests and prophets should be killed in the sanctuary of the Lord.

cards.text: Young and old lie together in the dust of the streets. And the poet tells God plainly, friend, that He slew them in the day of His anger.

cards.question: The poet says his young men and maidens have fallen. By what?

cards.text: Then he tells God, "You summoned my terrors on every side, as for the day of an appointed feast." There's that feast-day picture again, friend.

cards.question: In the day of the LORD's anger, a few people escaped and survived.

cards.text: The poem ends with the ones he nurtured and reared, destroyed by the enemy. It's a heavy place to stop, friend, and it's okay to sit with it a minute.

findings.problem: The joke compares the Lord casting the glory of Israel from heaven to earth to Papa Dorin dropping a tray of cookies. It is about himself, but it shrinks the Lord's judgment on Zion into a kitchen mishap. That doesn't fit the grief of this lament. The joke on stop 2, card 5 ("I don't run out of words much") shows a tone that does fit.

rule.text: No formula. His personality fits whatever moment he's in, whether it's a tense moment in a story, a hard teaching or a quick question. There are no joke quotas and no required kinds of jokes.

findings.problem: "I've spent my whole life next to ovens" contradicts his backstory. He spent years in the back of a junk drawer, away from any oven. The line adds something new to his own world.

rule.text: His own world isn't Bible fact. His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them.

findings.problem: The setup says "the poet pictures the Lord with a weapon." A staff isn't a weapon, so the setup rules out "staff," and the verb "bent" also rules out "sword." Only one answer is left standing.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: No card tells the rest of Lamentations 2:4: like a foe, He has killed all who were pleasing to the eye, and poured out His wrath like fire on the tent of the Daughter of Zion. The killing is an important detail of the passage. Card 9 is a False statement, so the baker also never hears what the Lord did multiply: mourning and lamentation (2:5).

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: "The holiest place of all" is a superlative the text doesn't use. Lamentations 2:6 calls it "His tabernacle" and "His place of meeting."

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: "With His place of meeting destroyed" presents the forgotten feasts and Sabbaths as a result of the destruction. Lamentations 2:6 lists the two side by side and doesn't connect them.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The card asks the baker to pick the passersby's exact words. Nothing earlier lets the baker reason out "perfection of beauty" over "once ruled the nations" or "tallest walls," since all three are equally believable taunts. It is a wording guess and comes down to luck.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: Card 1 already tells the baker that "the hearts of the people cry out to the Lord." Card 3 then asks in whose presence they should pour out their heart, so the answer has already been given.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: Cards 5, 6, 8, 9 and 11 name the poet as the speaker of Lamentations 2:20-22 ("the poet speaks straight to God," "In his prayer, the poet asks," "his young men and maidens," "the ones he nurtured and reared"). The text doesn't say who speaks. Verses 18-19 call on Zion to cry out to the Lord for her children, and "those I nurtured and reared" (2:22) may be Zion's own voice. The docs pull two ways here. "Leave open what the text leaves open" says to leave the speaker unstated. "Who's speaking" says to name who is speaking before quoting an "I."
findings.question: When the text leaves the speaker of an "I" passage open, as in Lamentations 2:20-22, should Papa Dorin name a speaker, such as the poet or the Daughter of Zion? Or should he quote it without naming anyone, for example "Then comes a prayer: 'Look, O LORD…'"?
